steps.body: Symmetry hides in everyday letters too. Using standard block capital letters: **A** has a vertical line of symmetry (left-right mirror). **H** has both a vertical AND a horizontal line. **F** has none at all.

widget.prompt: Sort each block capital letter by its symmetry.

items.label: A
items.feedback: A's left and right halves mirror each other — vertical only.

items.label: H
items.feedback: H matches left-right AND top-bottom — both.

items.label: F
items.feedback: F's top and bottom halves are completely different shapes — no line symmetry.

items.label: O
items.feedback: A round O matches left-right AND top-bottom — both.

widget.missFeedback: Picture folding the letter each way — does either fold (or both) produce a match?
widget.successFeedback: A is vertical-only; H and O are both; F has no line of symmetry at all.

predict.prompt: Does the block capital H have MORE than one line of symmetry?
predict.reveal: H folds onto itself both vertically and horizontally — two mirrors in one letter. Some letters are richer in symmetry than they look.

explanationVariants: T's left and right halves mirror each other perfectly — vertical symmetry.
A vertical fold down the middle of T produces a match.

widget.prompt: Does the block capital letter T have a vertical line of symmetry?

options.label: Yes — folding down the middle matches both halves
options.feedback: T's left and right sides mirror each other exactly.

options.label: No — the top bar makes it uneven
options.feedback: The top bar is centered and even on both sides — folding down the middle DOES produce a match.

options.label: Only if it's written in cursive
options.feedback: This lesson uses standard block capital letters, where T's vertical fold clearly matches.

options.label: Only the horizontal fold works for T
options.feedback: A horizontal fold of T would NOT match (the top bar and the tall stem are very different). It's the VERTICAL fold that works.

steps.body: Watch out for a trap: the letter **N** looks like it might have symmetry because spinning it 180° looks the same. But that's **rotational** symmetry (a spin), a completely different idea from **line** symmetry (a fold). No single fold line makes N's two halves match.

explanationVariants: N looks the same after a 180° spin, but that's rotational symmetry — no fold line makes its two halves match.
Spinning and folding test two different, unrelated things.

widget.prompt: The letter N looks the same when spun upside down (180°). Does N have a LINE of symmetry?

options.label: No — that's rotational symmetry, a different idea from folding
options.feedback: Looking the same after a spin is rotational symmetry. No fold line makes N's two halves match — it has no line of symmetry.

options.label: Yes — looking the same after spinning counts as symmetry
options.feedback: Spinning and folding are different tests. N passes the SPIN test (rotational) but fails the FOLD test — no line of symmetry.

options.label: Yes — through its diagonal stroke
options.feedback: Folding along N's diagonal stroke doesn't make the two halves match up as mirror images — that's still the spin property, not a fold.

options.label: It depends on how the N is drawn
options.feedback: For any standard N shape, folding never produces a true mirror match — its apparent symmetry is specifically the rotational kind.

widget.prompt: Sort each real-world object: does it have a line of symmetry, or not?

items.label: A plain paper heart shape
items.feedback: A heart folds perfectly down the middle — a classic symmetric shape.

items.label: A shoe (just the left shoe, by itself)
items.feedback: A single shoe's inner and outer sides are shaped differently — no fold matches them.

items.label: A plain water glass, viewed from the front
items.feedback: A symmetric glass folds evenly down its center.

items.label: A number 7
items.feedback: A standard 7 has no fold that produces matching halves.

widget.missFeedback: Picture folding the object down a candidate line — do the two sides truly match?
widget.successFeedback: Hearts and glasses fold into matching halves; a single shoe and the number 7 don't.

steps.body: A shape from earlier in this course.
explanationVariants: A square, with all four sides and angles equal, has 4 lines of symmetry — matching the pattern from the last lesson.
Recalling the regular-shape rule: 4 sides, 4 symmetry lines.

widget.prompt: Recall: a square has 4 equal sides. How many lines of symmetry does it have?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 is a non-square rectangle's count. A square's equal sides give it the full 4 lines of symmetry.
1 undercounts significantly. A square, with all sides equal, has 4 lines of symmetry.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A square is a regular shape — its symmetry count matches its 4 sides.

hints: This road sign is shaped like an equilateral triangle — all three angles are 60°.
Recall from earlier in this course: 60°, 60°, 60° classifies as an acute triangle.
An equilateral triangle's symmetry count matches its 3 equal sides.
explanationVariants: The sign's equilateral triangle shape (angles 60°-60°-60°, an acute triangle) has 3 equal sides, giving it 3 lines of symmetry.
3 equal sides means 3 symmetry lines, regardless of the triangle's acute classification — both facts come from the same equal-sided shape.

widget.prompt: A road sign is shaped like an equilateral triangle, with all three angles measuring 60° (which you learned classifies it as an acute triangle). How many lines of symmetry does this triangle have?

commonErrors.feedback: 1 would be right for an isosceles triangle with only two equal sides. This triangle has all THREE sides equal, giving it 3 lines of symmetry.
60 is the degree measure of each angle, not the symmetry-line count. With 3 equal sides, this triangle has 3 lines of symmetry.

widget.fallbackFeedback: An equilateral triangle's 3 equal sides give it 3 lines of symmetry.

steps.body: Every shape and letter, folded and checked.
takeaways: Letters can have vertical symmetry, horizontal symmetry, both, or none — check with the fold test.
Rotational symmetry (spinning) and line symmetry (folding) are different ideas — don't mix them up.
The regular-shape pattern (sides = symmetry lines) applies everywhere, from road signs to windows.
steps.teaser: That's every skill Lines & Angles set out to teach — points, rays, and angles; parallel and perpendicular; classifying shapes; and now symmetry. With this course complete, every course in Grade 4's original map is now live.

concept.body: Quick rewind. **Fold-test each letter or object separately for vertical and horizontal symmetry.** The letter M: folding it down the middle (vertical) matches both halves. Folding it top-to-bottom (horizontal) does not — M is vertical-only.

explanationVariants: M's left and right halves mirror each other — vertical symmetry only.
The vertical fold works; the horizontal fold does not.

widget.prompt: Does the block capital letter M have a vertical line of symmetry?

options.label: Yes
options.feedback: M's left and right halves mirror each other perfectly.

options.label: No
options.feedback: M's two peaks are evenly spaced — folding down the middle DOES produce a match.

options.label: Only horizontally
options.feedback: M's top and bottom don't match if folded horizontally. It's the VERTICAL fold that works.
